#4321. Congress just passed a major e-bike safety law. Here’s what it actually means

E-bike battery safety standards that have largely been voluntary across the US are on the verge of becoming mandatory federal requirements, following the passage of a major piece of legislation in Congress.

The US Senate unanimously passed H.R. 973, known as the Setting Consumer Standards for Lithium-Ion Batteries Act, on November 19. The House previously passed the bill in April 2025 by a 365-42 vote. The legislation now heads to the president for a signature.

So what does that actually mean for e-bikes and their batteries?

The biggest change is that the Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) would be required to turn three widely used UL safety standards into mandatory federal consumer product safety standards. Those include UL 2271 for light electric vehicle batteries, UL 2849 for e-bike electrical systems, and UL 2272 for personal e-mobility devices such as electric scooters.

Currently, those standards are generally voluntary at the federal level, though some jurisdictions have already made them mandatory. New York City, for example, requires certification to applicable UL standards for e-bikes, batteries, and other micromobility devices sold in the city.

If H.R. 973 becomes law, that approach would effectively go nationwide.

The bill gives the CPSC 180 days after enactment to promulgate the three standards as final consumer product safety standards. And this isn’t simply a one-time requirement based on today’s standards. Future revisions would generally become federal requirements 180 days after the CPSC is notified, unless the agency determines that a revision doesn’t improve safety.

For established e-bike companies already selling UL-certified products, the immediate impact may be relatively small. Many major brands have already moved toward UL 2849 certification, particularly as retailers and municipalities have increasingly demanded it.

The bigger impact is likely to be felt at the lower end of the market, where inexpensive e-bikes, replacement batteries, and direct-import products have continued to enter the US without certification to recognized safety standards.

Importantly, UL certification isn’t a guarantee that a lithium-ion battery can never catch fire. Damage, improper repairs, incompatible chargers, manufacturing defects, and other problems can still create hazards.

But the standards are designed to test batteries and electrical systems against foreseeable electrical, mechanical, and environmental stresses. Making those standards mandatory would establish a nationwide minimum safety floor instead of leaving compliance largely voluntary.

I’d say that’s probably the biggest change here: we aren’t talking about a new e-bike technology or a new battery chemistry. We’re talking about taking safety standards that much of the reputable e-bike industry already follows and making them the baseline for everyone selling these products in America.

#4319. A simple metal is hiding a strange new form of magnetism

A surprisingly simple metal has revealed an unusual form of magnetism that could open new possibilities for quantum technology. Researchers have found compelling evidence of a rare magnetic state in which electrons behave in unexpected ways, even though the material produces no overall magnetization.

The material, known as europium silicide (EuSi), contains an intricate magnetic structure that influences how electrons move and how their spins are oriented. This behavior is associated with a phenomenon called p-wave magnetism, an emerging area of research that could eventually help scientists develop new approaches to controlling electronic properties.

The discovery is particularly significant because EuSi is a relatively simple metallic compound. Unlike many materials previously considered for studying this exotic form of magnetism, it offers researchers a practical way to investigate the underlying physics in detail.

An Unexpected Discovery in a Simple Metal

The research began about three years ago at the Max Planck Institute for Chemical Physics of Solids (MPI CPfS) in Dresden, Germany. Dr. Erjian Cheng successfully grew high-quality single crystals of EuSi, providing the material needed for detailed experiments.

When researchers first examined the crystals using photoemission techniques, which probe the energies and behavior of electrons inside materials, they noticed something unexpected. The magnetic arrangement of the atoms had a remarkably strong influence on the electronic band structure, which describes the energy levels electrons can occupy and helps determine how a material conducts electricity.

That observation raised an intriguing possibility. Could this simple compound contain an unconventional form of magnetism in which the spin of an electron is connected to the direction it travels?

"When we first measured the electronic structure of EuSi, we were surprised by the exceptionally large effect of magnetism on the electrons," explains Cheng. "That observation led us to investigate whether this simple compound could host a much more unusual magnetic state. The combination of crystal growth, neutron scattering and spin-resolved spectroscopy now provides compelling evidence for p-wave magnetism."

Answering that question required an international collaboration involving 38 scientists from 19 institutions. Participants included researchers from ShanghaiTech University, the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, the Max Planck Institute for the Physics of Complex Systems and Oak Ridge National Laboratory.

A Strange Form of Magnetism That Cancels Itself Out

Ordinary magnets, such as those attached to refrigerators, typically rely on a magnetic arrangement called ferromagnetism. In these materials, many electron spins align in the same direction, producing an overall magnetic field.

At temperatures between approximately 33 and 62 kelvin, the magnetic moments of its europium atoms organize themselves into a repeating spiral pattern. These temperatures correspond to roughly minus 400 to minus 348 degrees Fahrenheit.

Each europium atom has a substantial magnetic moment, but their orientations balance one another across the spiral. As a result, the material has no net magnetization in this magnetic phase.

However, the absence of overall magnetization does not mean magnetism has stopped influencing the electrons. In fact, the researchers found that the spiral arrangement produces a highly unusual electronic structure.

In the proposed p-wave magnetic state, electrons traveling in opposite directions have opposite spin polarizations. Electron spin is a quantum property that gives electrons magnetic characteristics, although it should not be understood as an electron literally spinning like a tiny ball.

The relationship between an electron's direction of motion and its spin is called an odd-parity spin texture. This means that reversing the electron's momentum also reverses the associated spin polarization.

Other materials can display spin-dependent energy differences because of a phenomenon known as spin-orbit coupling, which connects an electron's motion to its spin. In EuSi, however, the unusual spin structure appears to arise mainly from interactions between magnetic moments and the specific symmetry of their spiral arrangement.

Experiments Reveal Evidence of Rare P-Wave Magnetism

To determine whether EuSi truly exhibits the predicted magnetic state, the scientists combined several sophisticated experimental methods with theoretical calculations.

First, they used neutron diffraction, a technique that reveals how atoms and magnetic moments are arranged inside a material. These measurements confirmed that the europium magnetic moments form a spiral structure with the symmetry required for p-wave magnetism.

Next, the researchers examined the material using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. This method measures the energies and momenta of electrons, allowing scientists to map the electronic structure.

The results showed that magnetic ordering substantially reorganizes the electron energy levels. In particular, the team observed magnetically driven energy separations exceeding 100 millielectronvolts, indicating an unusually strong influence of magnetism on electron behavior.

The most decisive evidence came from spin-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, which allowed the researchers to examine electron spin polarization directly.

They observed that the sign of the spin polarization changed across successive magnetic Brillouin zones. These zones are regions of momentum space used by physicists to describe how electrons behave within a repeating magnetic structure.

The team also found that spin polarization became much weaker near locations where theoretical calculations predicted the p-wave spin texture should disappear.

Taken together, the measurements provide compelling experimental evidence consistent with the predicted p-wave magnetic state in EuSi.

A Hidden Magnetic Spiral With Two Different Orientations

The researchers uncovered another unusual feature of EuSi involving chirality, a scientific term describing handedness.

A familiar example is the difference between a left hand and a right hand. They are mirror images, but they cannot be perfectly superimposed.

Something similar happens with the magnetic spiral inside EuSi. Although the underlying crystal has a centrosymmetric structure, meaning its atomic arrangement is unchanged by inversion through a central point, the magnetic spiral can twist in either of two opposite directions.

These different spiral orientations create magnetic regions, or domains, with opposite handedness.

Using magnetic force microscopy and spatially resolved photoemission spectroscopy, the scientists identified domains measuring approximately ten micrometers across. For perspective, ten micrometers is about one-tenth the thickness of a typical human hair.

When the researchers examined these regions using circularly polarized light, they detected different electronic responses depending on the handedness of the magnetic spiral.

This finding demonstrates that the direction in which the magnetic structure twists is linked to the material's electronic properties.

"What makes EuSi particularly exciting is that an unconventional electronic spin structure emerges from the magnetic order of a chemically simple metal," says Prof. Claudia Felser, Director at MPI CPfS. "This demonstrates how the discovery of new materials can reveal entirely new electronic phenomena. EuSi now gives us an experimental platform to investigate how magnetic symmetry and chirality can be used to control electronic properties, with potential implications for future spintronics and unconventional superconductivity."

Why This Discovery Matters for Quantum Technology

One of the biggest challenges in studying p-wave magnetism has been finding materials that display the necessary magnetic properties while remaining practical for detailed experiments.

Earlier candidates have included insulating materials, as well as metals that develop the required magnetic order only at extremely low temperatures or have complicated symmetries that make their behavior difficult to interpret.

EuSi offers a particularly useful combination of characteristics.

It is a stoichiometric metal, meaning its constituent elements occur in a fixed chemical ratio. Researchers can also grow high-quality single crystals of the material, and its spiral magnetic arrangement has the symmetry associated with p-wave magnetism.

Together, these features make EuSi a promising experimental platform for exploring how exotic magnetic states influence the behavior of electrons.

Theoretical studies suggest that metallic p-wave magnets could display several remarkable properties. For example, they may allow electrons with particular spin orientations to carry electrical currents without requiring an external magnetic field.

They could also produce strong changes in spin polarization when an electric current is applied, potentially offering new ways to manipulate electronic behavior.

These possibilities are especially relevant to spintronics, a field of technology that seeks to use electron spin, rather than electrical charge alone, to process and store information.

Another intriguing possibility involves unconventional superconductivity, in which electrical current flows without resistance through superconducting states that differ from those found in conventional superconductors.

Importantly, these predicted effects have not yet been demonstrated in EuSi. The discovery does not establish that the material can already perform these functions, but it gives researchers a promising system in which to test the predictions.

More broadly, the findings highlight how much of a material's behavior can remain hidden beneath an apparently simple chemical composition.

A solid's properties depend on more than the elements it contains or how its atoms are positioned. The arrangement of magnetic moments, the symmetries they create, and the quantum behavior of electrons can also produce entirely unexpected effects.

By revealing compelling evidence of p-wave magnetism in EuSi, researchers have gained a new opportunity to investigate these relationships and explore how unusual magnetic structures might eventually be used to control the electronic properties of future materials.

#4318. Battlefield 6's latest update dubbed the game's simultaneously best and worst patch as it runs into all kinds of issues

What's likely going to be the last major Battlefield 6 update of the year has launched with a number of unexpected issues.

There’s been a lot of anticipation for Battlefield 6’s version 1.1.3.0 patch. The patch kicks off the third and final phase of the game’s first season, adding some new holiday-themed content. More the new content itself, the update’s biggest additions are almost entirely gameplay-related.

Unfortunately, for as much as the changes in 1.1.3.0 have been well received, the launch has been marred by a series of technical issues, some of which are a little unusual.

Immediately after patch 1.1.3.0 went live, players on PC started reporting massive stutters that would occur every few seconds. The issue is especially pronounced in Redsec Battle Royale, but much deadlier in traditional multiplayer.

Battlefield Studios quickly acknowledged it, pointing out a workaround that appears to be working for players on Steam. According to those players, going offline on Steam’s friends menu has fixed stuttering for them.

The issue remains for other players on PC, however, and the developer said it’s working on a proper fix.

Perhaps the most disrupting problem the patch has caused is one that prevents players from being able to interact with the game’s menu. Tiles become unresponsive, or outright unselectable when you try to hover near them.

Ironically, the top set of tiles designed to make it easy for players to quickly jump into the new content has been the most affected. Restarting the game sometimes fixes the issue, and some players report that it only happens upon first launch after installing the update.

But Battlefield Studios later clarified that, unsurprisingly, there’s an actual reason behind the bug. Once again, a fix is being investigated, and the developer will offer an update once some progress has been made.

A little further down the list of importance is an issue that stops players from being able to skip tiers within the new Winter Offensive bonus path in the game’s battle pass. BF Studios took out the feature entirely while it works on a fix, so while you can continue making progress in the bonus path, you won’t be able to skip tiers.

This is all a shame to see. Outside of all the problems, the meat of the new update has been almost universally praised. The visibility improvements, and netcode updates have been celebrated. Many players were also happy to see meaningful updates to footstep audio and overall clarity.

It’s also unusual for a Battlefield 6 patch to run into so many issues at launch. The sentiment around 1.1.3.0 so far is that it’s the game’s best and worst update yet. Hopefully those issues will be fixed before the development team breaks for the holidays.

#4316. Cannabis users develop psychosis years earlier, and the gap grows with age

A major international analysis has found that people who use cannabis experience their first episode of psychosis about two and a half years earlier, on average, than those who do not use the drug. Even more concerning, the difference becomes substantially larger with age, reaching more than six years among people who develop psychosis in their 30s or later.

The findings, published in the journal Biological Psychiatry, come from researchers at UNSW Sydney. They suggest that the potential psychiatric consequences of cannabis use may extend well beyond adolescence and could become more pronounced with prolonged exposure.

Psychosis is a condition in which a person experiences a disruption in their perception of reality. Symptoms can include hallucinations, false beliefs known as delusions, and disturbances in thinking or behavior. It can occur in schizophrenia and several other mental health disorders. Although psychosis most commonly begins during the late teenage years or early adulthood, it can develop at other stages of life. According to Psychosis Australia, up to 3% of adults will experience a diagnosed disorder involving psychosis during their lifetime.

Cannabis Linked to Earlier Psychosis Across Adulthood

To investigate the relationship between cannabis use and the timing of psychosis, researchers at UNSW Medicine analyzed 149 studies involving more than 71,000 participants. Most of the research had been conducted since 2011 in Europe, North America, and Australia, with the majority of studies focusing on people diagnosed with schizophrenia.

The researchers discovered that the difference in the age at which psychosis first appeared varied considerably across age groups.

In studies where the average age of psychosis onset was between 20 and 24, cannabis users experienced their first episode approximately 1.6 years earlier than non-users. That difference widened to 4.43 years in studies involving people whose psychosis emerged in their mid-to-late 20s (25-29).

The largest difference appeared in studies where psychosis developed at age 30 or later. In this group, cannabis users experienced the condition an average of 6.3 years earlier than non-users.

These results suggest that the association between cannabis and earlier psychosis may become stronger as people grow older, potentially reflecting the effects of longer periods of cannabis exposure.

Chief investigator Matthew Large, a psychiatrist and Conjoint Professor at UNSW's School of Clinical Medicine, said the findings raise important questions about the long-term psychiatric effects of cannabis.

"We've tended to focus on the dangers of using cannabis in adolescence, when the brain is still developing, but the risk doesn't disappear once you're in your 20s," Prof. Large said. "What we're seeing suggests a cumulative effect, where harm builds up over time, a bit like alcohol or nicotine."

Interestingly, the analysis did not identify a statistically significant difference in the timing of psychosis between teenage cannabis users and teenagers who did not use cannabis.

However, the researchers cautioned that this finding does not necessarily mean younger cannabis users face no risk. Psychosis rarely develops before the middle teenage years, leaving relatively little opportunity for its onset to shift to an even younger age.

"There may be a biological floor, in that there is only so much earlier that onset can be shifted. In younger groups, strong development, genetic or other psychosis risk factors may dominate, making any cannabis-related age shift harder to detect," Prof. Large said.

The researchers also stressed an important limitation. Because the analysis examined existing observational studies, it cannot establish that cannabis directly causes psychosis or makes the condition begin sooner. Demonstrating such a relationship experimentally would require research that deliberately exposed people to potential psychiatric harm, which would be unethical.

Nevertheless, Prof. Large believes the overall pattern provides meaningful evidence supporting a possible causal connection.

"But the consistency of the evidence, particularly the strong effect in older adults who likely have been using cannabis for longer, does support the theory that cannabis plays a causal role in the timing of psychosis onset, and possibly the onset of some cases among people who would not have otherwise developed psychosis."

New Findings Challenge Assumptions About Cannabis After Age 25

The latest research builds on two earlier investigations into cannabis use and the development of psychosis.

In a smaller 2011 meta-analysis led by Prof. Large, researchers found that psychosis began approximately 2.7 years earlier among cannabis users. A separate 2015 analysis reported that psychosis typically developed 6.3 years after cannabis use began.

However, neither earlier investigation had enough information to determine how the relationship differed across age groups.

By incorporating a much larger body of research, the new analysis allowed scientists to examine how the association changes across different stages of adulthood.

Lead author Carly Stevens, from UNSW's School of Biomedical Sciences, said the findings undermine the idea that avoiding cannabis during adolescence is sufficient to eliminate its potential psychiatric dangers.

"What we've found challenges the assumption that you'll be fine if you wait to smoke weed until your mid-20s; that's just not the case," Ms. Stevens said.

"There's been so much emphasis on adolescents not smoking cannabis, which is important, but we need to broaden the warnings for everyone."

Why Even a Few Years of Delayed Psychosis Matter

Although a difference of two or three years might initially seem relatively small, the researchers emphasized that the timing of psychosis can have profound consequences for a person's future.

The late teenage years and early adulthood are often periods when people complete their education, begin careers, establish relationships, and develop greater independence. Experiencing a serious psychiatric disorder earlier in life can interrupt these important milestones.

"People may miss out on study, job opportunities, travel, and relationships in those years, and treatment can come with physical side effects that can make life harder as well," Ms. Stevens said.

Prof. Large emphasized the potential benefits of reducing or discontinuing cannabis use and the importance of delaying the onset of psychosis wherever possible.

"It's a major illness, which robs you of your shared reality with family, friends and all those around you," he said. "If we can delay psychosis by even a few years, people will be more likely to reach crucial milestones in education and training, and develop strong support networks, which can protect against psychosocial decline."

The potential benefits could also extend to healthcare systems. According to Prof. Large, psychotic disorders account for as much as 3% of health-related spending in developed countries. Preventing or delaying the onset of these conditions could therefore have substantial social and economic benefits.

Scientists Call for Stronger Cannabis Health Warnings

Despite the inability to establish a direct cause-and-effect relationship, the researchers believe their findings provide sufficient justification for stronger warnings about the possible psychiatric consequences of cannabis use.

"We can't run direct experiments, so we have to go with the best evidence available," Prof. Large said. "In my view, the threshold for health warnings about cannabis and psychosis has definitely been met."

One concern is the growing popularity of medical cannabis. Prof. Large said its increasing use as a therapeutic product may encourage some people to assume that it carries little risk.

He has also observed an increasing number of patients receiving treatment for psychosis who had previously been prescribed cannabis for medical conditions where evidence supporting its effectiveness remains limited.

"It's got this therapeutic halo around it, which blinds people to the risk."

Another emerging concern involves cannabis edibles, which can contain elevated concentrations of Tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the main compound responsible for the drug's mind altering effects. The availability of products containing higher THC concentrations raises additional questions about possible psychiatric risks.

At the same time, Prof. Large acknowledged that cannabis legalization could create opportunities to reduce harm, even though it would also make cannabis easier to obtain.

Legal regulation could allow governments to establish limits on product potency, improve consumer education, introduce taxation, and require buyers to receive clear information about potential health consequences.

"You could tax it, regulate it, and require people to show they understand the risks before buying," Prof. Large said.

More Research Needed on Long-Term Cannabis Exposure

The researchers say further studies are necessary to understand the biological processes that might explain why the association between cannabis use and earlier psychosis becomes more pronounced with age.

In particular, they want to investigate whether repeated or prolonged cannabis exposure produces cumulative changes that influence when psychotic symptoms emerge.

They also recommend additional research focusing on older cannabis users, an increasingly important population as medical cannabis becomes more common and products containing high concentrations of THC become more widely available.

Another priority is improving how cannabis exposure is measured. The researchers argue that future studies need clearer and more consistent methods for recording cannabis consumption so that findings can be compared more reliably.

Ultimately, the new analysis highlights an important gap in public understanding of cannabis and mental health. While warnings have traditionally concentrated on teenage use, the findings suggest that potential psychiatric risks deserve attention throughout adulthood, particularly among people who continue using cannabis over many years.

#4315. 2027 Toyota 4Runner Starts over $45,000 for the First Time

Every 4Runner now costs more than last year, but the base-level SR5’s $1220 price hike is the steepest.

The Toyota 4Runner’s starting price will clear $45,000 for the first time ever. That comes after the base-level SR5 trim receives a $1220 price increase, bringing the least expensive 4Runner up to $45,085. While every trim has increased in price, the SR5’s rise is the most substantial.

To help offset the upcharge, the base model now features standard heated front seats. The driver and front passenger seats also get standard eight-way power adjustments. Previously, heated seats were standard on the next-step TRD Sport trim, which started at $50,345 and featured six-way manual buckets. However, if you’re someone who muscles through long, cold winters and enjoys a heated backside, the $1220 price hike might feel like a discount when stacked against last year’s options.

See all results for used cars for sale near 37040

For the 2027 model year, the TRD Pro adds standard red-painted front tow hooks and an exclusive Hot Honey color, which is available for an extra $695. The Platinum trim now features standard puddle lamps that project the 4Runner logo on the ground when the front doors are opened. Also, the Black exterior color has been renamed “Inked” on all trim levels. Fancy stuff.

Beyond those tweaks, several trims roll into 2027 unchanged. However, prices are up across the board. Most trims have increased by about $200, but the hybrid version of the Platinum sees a steeper climb, costing $490 more than last year. The TRD Sport, TRD Off-Road, and hybrid TRD Off-Road have all increased by $870.

Four-wheel drive still comes standard on most trims, but it’s available for an extra $2000 on the SR5, TRD Sport, TRD Sport Premium, and Limited trims, just like last year. All 4Runners use a 278-hp turbocharged 2.4-liter four-cylinder with an eight-speed automatic transmission, and hybrid models add an electric motor to make 326 horsepower.

Every 4Runner is equipped with Toyota Safety Sense 3.0, which includes a host of driver assists such as lane-departure warning, adaptive cruise control, pedestrian detection, and road-sign assist. The base 2027 4Runner SR5 starts at $45,085, while hybrid models start at $55,945. New 4Runners are available to order now, with vehicles slated to reach dealerships toward the end of this year.

#4314. Arc Raiders gets a few map exploit fixes in latest patch as Embark prepares to slow down how often patches are released

There's a new Arc Raiders patch that's fairly small, but one with fixes everyone is going to appreciate.

The time has arrived for another Arc Raiders update, and Embark has certainly delivered. Today’s patch, version 1.6.0, is among the smallest the game has received so far, focusing almost exclusively on disabling map exploits.

Perhaps more important than the patch itself, however, is the announcement the developer made around it.

Starting off with patch 1.6.0, it takes out a particular zipline on Stella Montis, the game’s most recent addition ot the map roster. Some players used said zipline to get out of bounds, something the game has been battling on several of its maps.

On Blue Gate, the patch fixes a collision issue that allowed players to vault through a wall, and fall to their death. The map fixes continue with another on Spaceport Launch Tower, which takes out a gap in collision that players have been able to shoot through.

The last change in this update affects gameplay feel around Arc enemies. Certain materials in the game’s world weren’t blocking their vision - or fire - when they should have, and this has now been fixed.

Alongside today’s patch, Embark also announced that going forward, we’re going to see fewer patches for Arc Raiders. The game has been getting updates almost every Thursday since it launched in late October.

Now that most of the major problems have been fixed, the studio is shifting to a slower patching cadence. Critical fixes will still be issued as soon as they’re developed, but don’t expect a patch each week going forward.

Embark also revealed that patch releases and in-game store rotations will now occur on Tuesdays. You should also expect the next few weeks to be quiet, as members of the team go on holiday breaks.

But, before everyone goes away, the game is going to get one more big update. The last item on Arc Raiders’ roadmap, revealed in early November, is the Cold Snap event. This is on track for Tuesday, bringing some new content alongside a few other fixes.

#4312. Scientists discover a hidden gut defense that could prevent colon cancer

A common antibody found throughout the digestive tract may provide an unexpected defense against colon cancer. Researchers at Rockefeller University have discovered that these immune molecules help regulate the growth of cells lining the intestine, potentially preventing the uncontrolled cell division that can lead to tumors.

In a study published in Nature, scientists found that mice missing a type of antibody known as immunoglobulin A (IgA) developed more than twice as many colon tumors as mice with normal levels of the antibody. The researchers also uncovered how this protection works. IgA attaches to cells along the intestinal lining and helps prevent them from multiplying too rapidly.

Even more promising, when the team administered IgA orally to mice that lacked the antibody, the animals no longer showed an elevated risk of developing tumors.

"One intriguing aspect of this work is that it shows how a natural defense in the gut restrains the cell division that can lead to cancer," says senior author Daniel Mucida, who leads Rockefeller's Laboratory of Mucosal Immunology. "Most cancer research focuses on trying to destroy a tumor that already exists, but what if we could intervene before tumors form?"

The findings may help explain why people with IgA deficiency, a condition in which the body produces little or none of this antibody, face a greater risk of colorectal cancer. They also offer new insight into how gut bacteria, immune defenses, and intestinal cells work together to influence cancer development, potentially even in people with otherwise healthy immune systems.

Why the Gut Contains So Much of This Antibody

IgA is one of the immune system's most abundant antibodies in the digestive tract, where it provides an important early defense against potentially harmful microbes. Unlike antibodies that recognize a single specific target, IgA can interact with many different kinds of gut bacteria and even certain healthy cells belonging to the body.

Scientists have known for decades that the intestines contain unusually large quantities of IgA. However, the reasons for its abundance, and the full range of functions it performs, have remained incompletely understood.

Mucida's laboratory investigates how the intestine manages two essential but sometimes competing responsibilities. It must defend the body against dangerous microorganisms while allowing nutrients from food to pass into the bloodstream. Earlier research from his team has also helped explain how immune cells in the digestive tract contribute to food intolerances and allergies.

For the new study, Gregory Donaldson, a former postdoctoral researcher at Rockefeller who is now an assistant professor at UCLA, set out to better understand how IgA interacts with intestinal bacteria and whether those interactions might influence the development of colon cancer.

"We know these antibodies bind bacteria and, by doing so, can shape the microbiome," he says. "And because IgA deficiency, which affects about 1 in 500 people in the U.S., is linked to colorectal cancer, I wondered whether these interactions might be relevant to the disease."

The microbiome is the community of microorganisms living in and on the body. In the intestines, these microbes perform important functions related to digestion and immune health, but certain bacteria can also contribute to disease under the wrong conditions.

Missing Gut Antibodies More Than Doubled Colon Tumors

To investigate IgA's protective effects, Donaldson compared mice that could not produce the antibody with mice that had normal IgA levels. Both groups were raised together, allowing the researchers to control for differences in food and exposure to microorganisms.

The results revealed a striking difference. Animals without IgA developed substantially more colorectal tumors than their counterparts, consistent with the increased colorectal cancer risk observed in humans with IgA deficiency.

The association was not limited to a single experimental setup. Researchers observed the same pattern using multiple models of colon cancer, strengthening the evidence that IgA plays a meaningful protective role.

"We found this was true for several different kinds of models of colon cancer, so that was a really convincing effect," says Donaldson.

The team then tested whether replacing the missing antibody could reverse the effect. When mice lacking IgA received oral doses of the antibody, their increased susceptibility to colon tumors disappeared.

This result suggested that IgA does more than simply accompany other protective processes in the intestine. Its presence appears to directly influence conditions that determine whether tumors develop.

Scientists Discover a Natural Brake on Cancer Cell Growth

To understand the mechanism behind this protection, the researchers examined epithelial cells, which form the inner lining of the intestine. These cells are particularly important because colon cancer begins when cells in this tissue undergo changes that allow them to grow uncontrollably.

The intestinal lining is constantly renewing itself. Older or damaged cells are replaced by new ones, making controlled cell division essential for keeping the digestive tract healthy. However, when the signals that regulate this process become disrupted, excessive growth can create opportunities for cancer to develop.

In mice without IgA, the researchers identified changes in gene activity associated with cell proliferation, the process through which cells divide and increase in number. Crucially, these changes appeared before any tumors became visible, suggesting that the antibody helps regulate an early step in cancer development.

"We assumed there must be some sort of receptor on the epithelial cells that was mediating this," Donaldson says.

The researchers suspected that IgA was interacting with a specific molecular structure on the surface of intestinal cells, allowing it to influence how those cells behaved.

Gabriella Lima dos Reis, the study's second author and a graduate student working in Gabriel Victora's laboratory, investigated a promising candidate called DMBT1.

DMBT1 is a receptor found on the surface of epithelial cells that can bind to IgA. Previous research had connected it to several types of cancer, but scientists had not established precisely how it functions in the development of colon tumors.

How Gut Bacteria and IgA Control Tumor Formation

Further experiments revealed that DMBT1 plays two very different roles depending on whether IgA is present.

When intestinal bacteria are present, DMBT1 activates signals that encourage epithelial cells to divide. This response is part of the normal activity of the intestinal lining, which must continually replace cells to maintain its protective barrier.

IgA helps keep that growth under control. When the antibody binds to DMBT1, it restrains the receptor's activity, effectively acting as a brake on cell proliferation.

Without IgA, however, DMBT1 signaling can continue without sufficient restraint. Intestinal cells then divide more rapidly than they should, increasing the likelihood that tumors will develop.

The researchers confirmed that this excessive growth depends on several interacting factors. When gut bacteria were absent, DMBT1 signaling was disabled, or normal amounts of IgA were available, epithelial cell division remained under control.

Together, these findings reveal how a common immune molecule helps maintain the delicate balance between necessary tissue renewal and potentially dangerous overgrowth.

"If IgA is missing, epithelial cells that are performing their normal function -- responding to bacteria by producing new cells -- can keep dividing unchecked, leading to cancer," Mucida says. "We think this homeostatic effect is IgA's main function. This was a big surprise."

Homeostasis refers to the body's ability to maintain stable, healthy conditions despite constant changes in its environment. In this case, IgA appears to support that balance by preventing normal intestinal cell renewal from becoming excessive.

A New Possibility for Preventing Colon Cancer

By identifying DMBT1's normal role in intestinal cells, the Rockefeller team has uncovered a potential target for future colon cancer prevention strategies.

Instead of waiting until a tumor develops and then attempting to destroy it, researchers may eventually be able to influence the biological signals that make tumors more likely to form.

"Based on the mechanism we discovered, perhaps we could influence epithelial cells to be less likely to develop into a tumor," Mucida says. "We know, for example, that having polyps increases your chances of getting colon cancer, so we think that there could be an opportunity to target this pathway after polyps are removed. Right now, there are no interventions available at that point."

Colon polyps are growths that develop along the inner lining of the large intestine. Although many are harmless, some can eventually become cancerous. Removing them during a colonoscopy can reduce cancer risk, but researchers are interested in finding additional ways to prevent future tumors from developing.

The newly identified IgA and DMBT1 pathway could offer one such opportunity, although additional research is needed to determine whether targeting it would be effective and safe in humans.

Could Beneficial Gut Bacteria Help Prevent Cancer?

The discovery also raises another intriguing possibility. Certain intestinal bacteria may actively help protect against cancer by influencing how epithelial cells behave or by encouraging the production of protective antibodies.

While much of the research into the gut microbiome and cancer has focused on harmful bacteria that promote tumor formation or accelerate cancer growth, some microbes may have the opposite effect.

"What is potentially even more exciting is that there is evidence that individual species of bacteria can have really specific effects on epithelial cells as well," Donaldson notes. "A lot of research has focused on bacteria that induce tumors or can exacerbate their growth, but we have some evidence that there are bacteria that could do the opposite, just as IgA does. To that end, perhaps we could develop a probiotic supplement that induces a protective IgA response. This is all very speculative, but it's one direction that we could look towards in the future."

Such an approach would aim to use beneficial microorganisms to stimulate the body's existing protective mechanisms rather than directly attacking cancer cells. However, the idea remains speculative, and the mouse experiments do not establish that taking IgA supplements or probiotics can prevent colon cancer in people.

For now, the findings provide a clearer picture of how the immune system and gut microbiome cooperate to maintain healthy intestinal tissue. They also suggest that some of the body's most important defenses against cancer may operate long before the disease becomes detectable.

Mucida adds, "Overall, there is a lot more to learn about how the dance between bacteria, antibodies, and epithelial cells in the gut works to maintain health."

#4311. Acura Makes Japanese-Market Debut with the U.S.-Built Integra Type S

The Integra Type S is now for sale in Japan, making it the first Acura-branded vehicle to reach the Japanese market.

The 2026 Acura Integra Type S is officially for sale in Japan. That might not seem like big news, considering Honda Motor Company is headquartered in Japan, but the release marks the first Acura-branded vehicle to be exported to the Japanese market. While this is Acura’s first time in Japan, it’s strangely not the Integra’s, which spent a few decades wearing a Honda badge from 1985 to 2006.

Most Acuras are designed and built in the United States and sold throughout North America. The new Integras for sale in Japan are the same as those sold stateside, meaning they’ll be left-hand-drive anomalies in a predominantly right-hand-drive market.

See all results for new 2027 Acura Integra Type S for sale near 23224

That also means they’ll get the same 320-hp turbocharged 2.0-liter inline-four that we’re quite fond of in the United States. The front-wheel-drive sport compact is only offered with a six-speed manual transmission and features a limited-slip differential, Brembo brakes, and 19-inch wheels wrapped in summer tires. The whole package comes together to reach 60 mph in a brisk 5.1 seconds.

Honda builds every Integra Type S at its assembly plant in Marysville, Ohio, and the engines come from Honda’s Anna Engine Plant, also located in Ohio. Honda began exporting vehicles from Ohio to Japan in 1988 and has shipped nearly 300,000 Hondas to Japan since then.

Honda says the Teg’s introduction in Japan marks a strong global demand for an enthusiast-centered performance sedan. If the Type S is well-received in the Japanese market, it’s likely that more Acuras could start making their way to Japan in the future. Pricing and the exact number of Integra Type S models available in Japan haven’t been released yet, but considering they’re identical to the Type S models sold on our shores, they’ll likely come in around $56,000.

#4310. This might be the real reason Elon Musk says Tesla’s AI5 chip is going to Optimus

Elon Musk says Tesla’s cars don’t need the next-generation AI5 chip, so it’s going to Optimus first. A new report from Taiwan’s chip supply chain gives a more practical reason: Tesla won’t have enough AI5 chips for its cars until 2028.

According to Commercial Times, Tesla’s chip design partner Global Unichip (GUC) is giving its limited TSMC 3nm capacity for 2027 to Google and Microsoft data center chips first. That leaves Tesla with a relatively small AI5 allocation.

Last Sunday, a Tesla owner asked Musk when AI5 would be in new cars. His answer: “It’s going to Optimus. Cars will remain at AI4. That’s enough to solve superhuman driving.”

As we reported this week, FSD v15 is basically AI4’s last shot. Tesla engineers are already squeezing the last few percent of utilization out of the chip, and the AI4.5 refresh is mostly a move to LPDDR5X memory. Musk said Tesla cut AI4.5 from 32GB to 24GB of RAM because “RAM is super expensive,” and that AI4 itself now costs twice as much due to memory and storage price hikes.

It’s quite a change in plans. In June 2024, Musk said AI5 would be in vehicles in the second half of 2025. Tesla only taped out AI5 in April, and Musk had already started describing its focus as Optimus and Tesla’s supercomputer clusters.

The Commercial Times report, published today, describes GUC as the custom ASIC design partner on Tesla’s AI5 project. GUC is the design services house whose largest shareholder is TSMC, and it works mostly on data center silicon.

Industry sources told the paper that GUC’s 2027 allocation of TSMC’s N3 capacity is much larger than this year’s. But with AI compute demand exploding, it still can’t serve every big customer at once.

So GUC is prioritizing North American cloud projects, including Google’s Axion 2 and Axion 3 server processors and Microsoft’s in-house chips. Those orders carry high margins and good visibility. Tesla’s robot and car chip doesn’t make the front of the line.

The result, according to the report, is that Tesla’s initial 2027 wafer quota can’t support annual shipments for a fleet of millions of cars. The supply chain expects that limited AI5 volume to go first to Optimus, which needs a lot of compute but ships in small numbers, and only expects large-scale adoption in cars after N3 capacity expands further in 2028.

TSMC is adding 3nm capacity, but not fast. Its new 3nm fab in Tainan is scheduled for volume production in the first half of 2027, and its second Arizona fab, which Musk has said will produce AI5, in the second half of 2027.

Tesla does have a second source. Samsung is building its own version of AI5 on 2nm at its Taylor, Texas fab, but it expects volume production of Tesla’s AI chips there in the second half of 2027.

Now look at the numbers. Tesla delivered roughly 1.6 million vehicles last year. Every one of them needs a self-driving computer.

Optimus is a different story. Tesla now plans to put AI5 in Optimus around April 2027 and push external Optimus deliveries to late 2027. Even an aggressive robot ramp next year is measured in thousands of units, not millions.

If your 2027 AI5 supply is a fraction of what a car program needs, Optimus is the only product Tesla has that can absorb it.

Musk’s version is that cars don’t need AI5 because AI4 is “enough to solve superhuman driving.” The supply chain’s version is that Tesla can’t get enough AI5 chips to put in cars anyway. Both can be true at the same time, but only one of them explains the timing.

Musk has made it clear that his top priority for Tesla autonomous driving is to be the cheapest to produce by a large margin. So he cut lidar and other sensors then designed the low cost to produce cybercab which also has low energy cost per mile. The only problem is that Musk hasn't prioritized operational autonomous driving.

Look at how Tesla has been handling silicon this fall. It cut AI4.5 RAM. It cut AI5 RAM from 144GB to 72GB, then bumped it to 96GB a day later. It says AI4 costs double what it used to. That’s a company rationing chips and memory, not one choosing to leave a 12x compute upgrade on the shelf because it isn’t needed.

And if AI4 really were plenty, Tesla engineers wouldn’t be talking about squeezing out the last few percent of the chip for v15.

So here’s how we read it. Tesla had to pick where its scarce AI5 chips go in 2027, and it picked the low-volume product. “AI4 is enough” is the story that makes that decision sound like a choice. And it’s a story we heard about HW3, Tesla’s previous self-driving computer.

#4309. Scientists discover a new type of depression that common antidepressants struggle to treat

A newly identified form of depression may help explain why some people struggle to find relief from commonly prescribed antidepressants. Researchers at the University of Sydney have discovered a subtype called "circadian depression," which appears to be closely connected to the body's internal biological clock.

The discovery emerged from an analysis of clinical and genetic information from more than 10,000 Australians with depression. Nearly one-quarter of the participants in the study, which focused on people with severe, recurrent or persistent depression, showed characteristics of this newly identified subtype.

Circadian depression is associated with the body's 24-hour internal clock, which helps regulate when we feel awake and when we feel sleepy. People with this form of depression tend to respond less favorably to common serotonin-based antidepressants. However, treatments that target the brain circuits involved in controlling circadian rhythms, including melatonin, melatonin-targeted antidepressants and light therapy, may offer more effective options.

Published in the British Journal of Psychiatry, the findings shed light on the genetic factors associated with this subtype and offer a possible explanation for why widely used medications such as SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) are less effective for some patients.

A Hidden Type of Depression Affecting Nearly One in Four Patients Studied

To investigate the biological differences between forms of depression, researchers examined information collected through the nationwide Australian Genetics of Depression Study. Their analysis included clinical histories and genetic data from more than 10,000 people who had experienced depression.

The researchers identified nearly 25 percent (2,604 participants) as having circadian depression. Several recognizable patterns distinguished these individuals from other people with depression.

Those with the circadian subtype were more likely to experience seasonal changes in their depression, sleep for longer periods when depressed, and wake up feeling exhausted despite spending more time in bed. They were also more likely to be night owls, meaning they naturally preferred staying awake late and waking later in the day.

The differences extended beyond sleep patterns. Depression often began earlier in life for these individuals, and their symptoms tended to be more severe (such as mania and higher levels of suicidal thoughts). Genetic analysis also revealed an increased predisposition to inflammatory and cardiovascular health problems, along with major neurodevelopmental disorders, including ADHD.

First author Dr. Emiliana Tonini from the University of Sydney's Brain and Mind Center said:

"Our research has identified circadian depression as a new subtype, affecting around a quarter of people in our study into those with severe, recurrent or persistent depression.

"Depression is not a uniform illness, and understanding the characteristics of different subtypes means that we can give people earlier access to treatments that will be most effective for them."

Why Common Antidepressants May Be Less Effective

One of the most important implications of the discovery involves how depression is treated.

Medications such as SSRIs and SNRIs (serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors) are generally among the first treatments offered to people diagnosed with depression. These drugs work by influencing chemical messengers in the brain that help regulate mood.

However, the researchers found that these medications tend to be less effective for people with circadian depression. Individuals with this subtype also experience more side effects, suggesting that conventional antidepressants may not be the best initial approach for everyone.

Because circadian depression is closely associated with the body's internal clock, therapies designed to influence that clock may be particularly useful. Light therapy, for example, uses controlled exposure to bright light to help regulate biological rhythms. Melatonin, a hormone involved in signaling when the body should prepare for sleep, and antidepressants that target melatonin pathways may also be relevant treatment options.

Co-senior author Dr. Jacob Crouse from the Brain and Mind Center explained:

"Because circadian depression is linked to people's internal body clock, treatments targeting the circadian rhythm, such as light therapy and melatonin, may be much more relevant, and clinicians should reach for these much earlier in people with this presentation.

"For those who find that antidepressants are not working for them, it is important to speak to your clinician for advice about your individual circumstances."

A New Approach Could Improve Depression Treatment in Young People

Recognizing circadian depression earlier could be especially important for younger patients, who may otherwise spend valuable time trying medications that are less suited to their particular form of depression.

Professor Ian Hickie, Co-Director of the Brain and Mind Centre and a clinical psychiatrist, warned that failing to identify this subtype in young people can contribute to unsuccessful early treatments and unnecessary side effects.

The findings highlight the importance of recognizing that depression is not a single, uniform condition. Different biological mechanisms may contribute to similar symptoms, meaning that treatments effective for one person may provide much less benefit to another.

By identifying patients whose depression is closely tied to circadian rhythms, clinicians may be able to offer more targeted treatments earlier rather than relying on the same initial medication approach for everyone.

"We really want young people to receive the most appropriate treatment early in their course of illness.

"Most young people will be offered SSRIs first up, but for at least a quarter there are better circadian-focused medical and behavioral options to help treat and manage their condition."

Materials provided by University of Sydney. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4307. Editor’s Letter: The Benz Patent Motorwagen Has Big Perambulator Vibes

I love new cars, but lately I’m fixated on cars of the past.

From the November/December 2026 issue of Car and Driver.

These days, I’m particularly interested in cars of the past. By that I mean the distant past. Such is the case for the 1886 Benz Patent Motorwagen I drove during Monterey Car Week. Now when someone asks, “What’s the oldest car you’ve ever driven?” I have an unassailable answer. That is, unless you’ve driven Cugnot’s steam car. You did? No way. Was it cool?

The Patent Motorwagen gets credit for being first because Carl Benz designed it to be a car from the get-go. He didn’t simply take a horse-drawn carriage, add an engine and drivetrain, subtract the horse and reins, carry the oats.

I love primordial stuff because things we take for granted today had not yet been figured out. There were lots of guesses—some right, others not. Driving a vehicle that old is disorienting, challenging, and sometimes dangerous. Maybe something will explode. Maybe you’ll fall out. Boring hadn’t been engineered into the experience yet.

See all results for used cars for sale near 14221

The Patent Motorwagen gives big perambulator vibes, and baby, I am here for it. It has only three wheels, to keep it simple and light. Carriages turned their entire axle, since uprights and kingpins at the wheels were still years away. Steering the first car involves grabbing what appears to be the wood handle of an awl—the automotive steering wheel hadn’t been invented yet either. Also not in existence in 1886: carburetor jets, engine radiators, radios, tetanus shots.

Another hitherto unimagined concept: hiding the crankshaft and flywheel behind casings. The crank, connecting rod, cam gear, and drive belt all sit out in the open. Some of those parts have to be greased up before your drive. For others, oil is metered out onto the cylinder and the intake valve by drip lubricators before it runs over less critical parts and leaves behind a greasy trail on the road.

To start the Benz, switch on the ignition that sends energy to the roughly eight-inch-long spark plug, then grab the horizontal flywheel. Give that a Wheel of Fortune–worthy spin and wait. The air-hexane fuel mixture is adjustable, so you can richen it to help the car start (it originally ran on naphtha, which was available at apothecaries in 1886, right next to the laudanum). There’s no throttle, so the 1.0-liter doesn’t stray far from its 400-rpm operating speed. A 4.8-quart copper vessel perched over the engine holds the water that cools the cylinder. After about an hour of operation, the water boils over, and you stop and take a calf’s-head-stew break to let things cool.

To accelerate, push the long lever on the left side of the leather-trimmed park bench to engage the engine-driven leather strap to the axle. Feel the 0.88 horsepower. To stop, pull that lever back to actuate a shoe that drags on the axle. Not to sound like an 1886 infomercial, but driving the Patent Motorwagen is so easy, a toddler could do it. It’ll hit a claimed 13 mph, and it was the most amazing 13 mph I’ve ever experienced. There’s no way I’m going to be this fun when I’m 140 years old.

See all results for used cars for sale near 14221

Senior features editor Elana Scherr shares my fondness for the supercentenarian set. She owns a 1915 Dodge, making her the perfect person to organize a U.S. equivalent of Britain’s London-to-Brighton race for early cars. I rode along and got to exceed a 45-mph speed limit in a 116-year-old Pullman, ancient proof that speed limits are set too low. Not to worry, I was running Waze. Scherr’s account begins on page 64.

If you aren’t in the mood to go antiquing, there’s a 795-hp Mustang on page 34, a nearly 1000-hp Audi super car on page 58, and the new Corvette Grand Sport on page 72. Encompassing both new and old, this is a great issue.

#4306. Hyundai’s new Mercury EV Concept will launch as the IONIQ M in 2027 [Images]

Hyundai unveiled the Mercury Concept, a preview of its upcoming entry-level electric SUV set to launch as the IONIQ M in 2027.

Following the IONIQ V, which went on sale in September, Hyundai offered a look at its upcoming IONIQ lineup for China at the Guangzhou Auto Show on November 27.

Hyundai’s Mercury Concept stole the spotlight. The concept previews its upcoming “B-segment premium smart SUV,” set to launch in China in 2027.

According to Hyundai, the IONIQ M will be “the most accessible entry-level model in the IONIQ universe.” Unfortunately, it’s designed specifically for China.

Like the IONIQ V, the electric SUV was developed by Hyundai Motor’s Chinese design and engineering team. As such, it features a unique style and advanced tech you won’t find in Hyundai’s vehicles sold in the US, Europe, or other overseas markets.

The SUV’s futuristic low-slung design is inspired by Mercury’s orbit around the sun. Up front, the shark-nose design and slim, edgy lights form Hyundai’s “H” badge, while an integrated rear spoiler adds to the compact, sporty look.

Hyundai said the production version will feature Zhuoyu L2++ ADAS and a high-tech cabin powered by ByteDance’s Doubao AI model.

A battery-swap version is also set to launch through Hyundai’s partnership with China’s CATL following the production IONIQ M.

The Mercury follows the Venus, now on sale as the IONIQ V, and the larger Earth SUV, as Hyundai’s third IONIQ Planet name designed for China. It will go on sale in 2027 as the IONIQ M, alongside the IONIQ V EREV.

In 2028, Hyundai will launch the production version of the Earth SUV, while two new energy vehicles will join the lineup in 2029.

Looks like a fantastic little car. Something like a Leapmotor B05 that I have been considering to replace our Golf and Passat, but it is hard to judge its size.

I hope it arrives here soon. The IONIQ 5 we have is great also but too big and too expensive to compete with Leapmotor, Xpeng, Geely, MG here.

While Hyundai didn’t reveal battery or powertrain specs, it will likely feature a similar setup to the IONIQ V.

The Hyundai IONIQ V is available in China with two CATL lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery packs: A 53.5 kWh battery paired with a 140 kW (188 hp) rear electric motor that offers a CLTC range of up to 540 km, or a 66.8 kWh battery paired with a 168 kW (225 hp) motor with a CLTC range of up to 650 km (404 miles).

Hyundai said the IONIQ M will be “the most accessible entry-level model in the IONIQ universe.” Given the IONIQ V starts at 109,900 yuan ($16,500), the production IONIQ M could be priced around 99,000 yuan ($15,000) in China.

#4303. Tested: New Lexus ES Hybrid Is Much Quicker Than the Old Version

With an extra 29 horsepower, it’s not an especially surprising result, though it is a welcome change.

Welcome to Car and Driver’s Testing Hub, where we zoom in on the test numbers. We’ve been pushing vehicles to their limits since 1956 to provide objective data to bolster our subjective impressions (you can see how we test here).

The debut of the 2026 Lexus ES brought a full overhaul to the luxury sedan, which included a revamped hybrid variant. The new generation comes with fresh styling, a longer wheelbase, and an updated powertrain. In our testing, a 2026 ES350h was considerably quicker than a 2023 Lexus ES300h F Sport Handling, which was the last ES hybrid we tested.

See all results for new 2026 Lexus ES for sale near 37040

In our recent test of the ES350h, the updated sedan sprinted to 60 mph in 6.6 seconds, while the 2023 car more or less jogged its way to the 60-mph mark in 7.9 seconds. That’s a huge improvement, and one that took us by surprise, given that the new car doesn’t look drastically more powerful than the old one on paper. That’s to say nothing of the additional 352 pounds of weight in the new car either.

So, where did all the extra quickness come from? Well, we can think of several places. For starters, the 2026 ES hybrid is more powerful, even if the numbers don’t jump off the page. The powertrain, which features a 2.5-liter four-cylinder engine, now churns out 244 horsepower, up from 215 in the 2023 ES. Along with a more powerful engine, the updated hybrid system uses a larger and more powerful electric drive motor than the previous generation. Lexus also now offers the gas-electric ES with all-wheel drive for the first time, and that’s the version we tested, with the additional traction helping offset the new car’s weight gain.

The new generation also moved from a 3.39:1 axle ratio to a 3.44:1 axle ratio, a change that increases low-end torque at the wheels and makes the newer car somewhat punchier off the line. Lastly, the 2026 car gets a larger hybrid battery that can provide more horsepower than the smaller unit in the previous ES.

None of the changes are individually earth-shattering—especially with the extra 352 pounds of weight—but add them together, and the ES hybrid is a much quicker car than before.

Jack Fitzgerald’s love for cars stems from his as yet unshakable addiction to Formula 1. After a brief stint as a detailer for a local dealership group in college, he knew he needed a more permanent way to drive all the new cars he couldn’t afford and decided to pursue a career in auto writing. By hounding his college professors at the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee, he was able to travel Wisconsin seeking out stories in the auto world before landing his dream job at Car and Driver. His new goal is to delay the inevitable demise of his 2010 Volkswagen Golf.

#4302. New gum disease treatment kills bad bacteria while sparing the good

Researchers in Japan have developed a promising new treatment for gum disease that kills harmful bacteria while leaving beneficial microbes unharmed. Unlike conventional approaches that can eliminate both good and bad bacteria, the new therapy is designed to target specific microbes responsible for damaging gums and the bone that supports teeth.

Developed by scientists at Nagoya University, the treatment combines antibodies obtained from egg yolks with near-infrared light. Early experiments in human cell cultures and mice suggest that it could offer a more precise way to combat periodontitis, a serious form of gum disease that can eventually lead to tooth loss. The findings were published in the Journal of Translational Medicine.

Why Conventional Gum Disease Treatments Can Cause Problems

The human mouth contains a complex community of microorganisms, many of which play important roles in maintaining oral health. Problems can arise when harmful bacteria multiply and disturb this delicate balance.

One particularly troublesome species is Porphyromonas gingivalis (P. gingivalis), which scientists classify as a keystone pathogen. This means it can have an outsized influence on the surrounding microbial community, even when it is not especially abundant. By promoting inflammation and disrupting the normal balance of oral bacteria, it can contribute to the destruction of the bone that holds teeth in place.

Treating periodontitis often involves eliminating the bacteria responsible for the infection. However, some existing antimicrobial treatments do not distinguish between harmful organisms and microbes that help maintain a healthy mouth.

"Current treatments for periodontitis, including antibiotics and antimicrobial photodynamic therapy (aPDT), eliminate both pathogenic and beneficial oral bacteria," said Kazuhide Sato, one of the corresponding authors and a lecturer at Nagoya University. "These approaches often disrupt the entire oral microbial ecosystem and can also release lipopolysaccharide (LPS), an endotoxin that may exacerbate inflammation."

Scientists Adapt Cancer Therapy to Target Gum Disease Bacteria

To overcome these limitations, the Nagoya University team turned to a technology originally designed to treat cancer. Known as near-infrared photoimmunotherapy, it uses antibodies linked to a light-sensitive dye to recognize specific targets. Once the compound attaches to its intended target, exposure to near-infrared light activates the dye and produces a damaging effect.

The researchers adapted this strategy to attack P. gingivalis without unnecessarily disturbing other oral bacteria. Their approach relies on IgY, a type of antibody collected from the egg yolks of hens that have been immunized against the pathogen.

Egg yolk antibodies offer a practical advantage because they can be produced in large quantities at relatively low cost. This could make them an attractive option for developing targeted treatments that are affordable and scalable.

The resulting technology, called near-infrared photo-antibacterial targeting therapy (NIR-PAT²), was developed by researchers at Nagoya University Graduate School of Medicine. The team included first author Hiroshi Maruyama, Professor Hideharu Hibi, and corresponding authors Sato and Kiyoshi Sakai.

To determine whether the treatment could destroy harmful bacteria while protecting healthy tissue, the researchers tested it in human cell cultures and mice. They also compared its effects with those of conventional antimicrobial therapies.

Light-Activated Antibodies Destroy Harmful Bacteria

Laboratory experiments showed that the antibody and dye combination attached specifically to P. gingivalis. Other bacterial species and healthy human gum cells were left unaffected.

When the researchers illuminated the targeted bacteria with near-infrared light, the activated dye damaged their outer membranes, ultimately killing them.

Microscopic examination revealed an important difference between this technique and conventional antimicrobial light therapy. Bacteria exposed to the new treatment developed tiny openings in their membranes but largely maintained their overall shape. By contrast, conventional antimicrobial photodynamic therapy caused the bacteria to break apart completely.

The distinction matters because destroying bacterial cells can release substances that contribute to inflammation. Preserving the overall structure of the targeted bacteria, even after killing them, could help limit this unwanted effect.

The researchers also examined how the treatments affected healthy human gum cells. Their targeted therapy caused no detectable harm to these cells, while conventional antimicrobial photodynamic therapy produced cellular damage and slowed healing.

The team next investigated whether these laboratory findings would translate into meaningful improvements in gum disease.

In mice with periodontitis, the experimental therapy significantly reduced the loss of alveolar bone, the part of the jawbone that surrounds and supports teeth. Preventing this type of bone deterioration is especially important because advanced periodontitis can loosen teeth and eventually cause them to fall out.

Analysis of the animals' saliva revealed another encouraging result. The treatment reduced P. gingivalis while preserving beneficial Streptococcus bacteria, helping maintain a healthier balance of microorganisms in the mouth.

Conventional antibiotics and antimicrobial photodynamic therapy, on the other hand, eliminated both harmful and beneficial bacteria in the experiments, causing broader disruption to the oral microbial community.

"Results demonstrated that, unlike antibiotics or standard light therapy, this approach selectively removes the primary pathogenic species while preserving the remainder of the oral bacterial community," Sato said.

Together, the findings suggest that targeting individual disease-causing bacteria could help control gum disease while avoiding some of the unintended consequences of broader antimicrobial treatments.

AI Could Help Develop More Precise Gum Disease Treatments

Although the early results are promising, the researchers recognize that periodontitis is a complex disease involving multiple bacterial species. Eliminating P. gingivalis alone may not be sufficient to treat every case.

To address this challenge, the team plans to use artificial intelligence (AI) to examine publicly available information about oral bacteria. By identifying other important microorganisms and studying how different species interact, they hope to uncover additional targets for future therapies.

The researchers also see potential implications beyond oral health. Periodontitis has been linked to several other medical conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis and diabetes.

Understanding the relationships between oral bacteria and these conditions could eventually help scientists identify which patients are most likely to benefit from specific treatments. AI analysis may play a role in making those decisions and guiding the development of more personalized approaches to gum disease.

For now, the therapy remains experimental, with its effectiveness demonstrated in laboratory studies and mice rather than human clinical trials. However, the findings point toward a possible future in which treating gum disease means selectively removing harmful bacteria instead of disrupting the entire microbial community that helps keep the mouth healthy.

#4301. Used Tesla Cybertruck prices jump after Musk kills it, one asks $150K

Used Cybertruck prices are up 10 to 15% in the month since Tesla announced it would end production of its electric pickup, according to listing data from CarGurus and Visor.

Some dealers are pushing it much further. One in New Jersey now wants $150,790 for a used Cyberbeast, about $36,000 more than Tesla charges for a brand-new one.

CarGurus’ price index puts the average used Cybertruck at $89,715, up 9.84% over the last 30 days and 13.5% over 90 days. Over the same 30 days, the broader used car market went down 1.37%.

Visor, which tracks dealer listings hourly and compares the same trucks month to month, shows a bigger move: +15% like-for-like versus last month, with an average asking price of $101,784 across 171 used trucks. Listings that sold in the last 30 days took 17 days on average.

The curve on CarGurus’ chart is flat at around $80,000 from July to late October. Then it bends up in November.

That lines up exactly with Tesla’s moves. On November 6, Musk said Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production at Giga Texas, and Tesla raised prices by up to 10% the same day. A week later, Tesla stopped selling every Cybertruck except the Cyberbeast at $109,990. And this week, it bumped the Cyberbeast again to $114,990, which is what Tesla’s configurator shows today.

In early August, the cheapest Cybertruck you could order was $69,990. Now it’s $114,990.

Sorting CarGurus’ nationwide used Cybertruck inventory by price, the top listing is a 2026 Cyberbeast with 4,493 miles at J&S AutoHaus in Ewing, New Jersey. The asking price is $150,790 with fees.

CarGurus flags it as “Overpriced” and says it’s $35,773 above market. But the price history is the best part.

The dealer listed it at $134,995 on November 20. It went to $139,995 on November 25, the day after Tesla’s latest $5,000 Cyberbeast hike, and then to $149,995 the next day. That’s $15,000 in six days on a truck nobody has saved yet, according to CarGurus.

The same dealer also has a 2026 Cyberbeast with 851 miles at $145,790. Elsewhere, a 2024 Cyberbeast with 302 miles in Calumet City, Illinois, is listed at $148,816. And a 2024 dual-motor AWD with 1,500 miles in Lincoln, Nebraska, is at $145,306. That’s more than the $99,990 Tesla charged for a fully loaded Foundation Series AWD back in 2024.

Canadian dealers are playing the same game. The most expensive listing on AutoTrader.ca right now is a 2024 Cyberbeast with 1 km in Mississauga at C$199,999. The other 13 priced listings in the country sit between C$105,000 and C$141,995.

Sort the same CarGurus inventory from the bottom, though, and the picture changes.

A 2025 AWD with 22,495 miles is listed at $68,619 in San Bernardino, California. A 2024 Cyberbeast with 65,482 miles is at $70,118. There are several 2024 AWD trucks with 20,000 to 40,000 miles in the $77,000 to $80,000 range, and CarGurus rates many of them as good or great deals.

So the floor didn’t move all that much. What moved is the top and the middle.

There’s another detail in the CarGurus data. The 2024 model year is up 11.68% in 30 days, to $91,220. The 2025 model year is flat at $80,979, with 0% change over the same period.

The 2024 trucks include the Foundation Series, which came with Tesla’s “Full Self-Driving” package bought outright. Tesla now only sells FSD as a subscription, so those trucks have something new ones don’t. The 2025s, mostly the cheaper AWD trims, aren’t getting the same bump.

It’s good news for current owners who want out. Many of them watched their trucks lose about half their value between 2024 and 2025. This is the best window they’ve had in a long time.

Um no. ASKING prices are up. Transaction prices? They will resume their cratering momentarily.

But we wouldn’t read it as a sudden wave of love for the Cybertruck. Tesla made the cheaper versions impossible to order, so used trucks are now the only way to get anything other than a $115,000 Cyberbeast. That pushes the middle of the market up. And part of it is just dealers testing what people will pay. These are asking prices.

The bigger question is what happens after production ends. Parts and service for a low-volume stainless-steel truck that Tesla no longer makes. We’d expect that to weigh on used values far more than a configurator price hike helps them.

If you own one and you’ve been thinking about selling, now looks like a good time. If you’re buying, don’t pay discontinuation hype prices.

#4300. Toyota confirms the Highlander 9X will launch as its first EREV with top-tier tech in early 2027

The Toyota Highlander 9X will go on sale in early 2027 as the brand’s first extended-range electric vehicle with advanced new tech from Huawei and CATL.

Toyota joins Hyundai Motor Group, including Kia and Genesis, Ford, Volkswagen, and several other major OEMs with plans to launch its first EREV in the first quarter of 2027.

Toyota’s Chinese joint venture, GAC Toyota, announced at the Guangzhou Auto Show on November 27 that the EREV will use its flagship SUV nameplate, the Highlander 9X, when it arrives.

The Highlander 9X will blend Toyota’s classic global car heritage with some of China’s most advanced technology.

At the event, GAC Toyota revealed that the flagship EREV will use a battery custom-developed through its partnership with CATL, along with Huawei’s advanced driver assistance system (ADAS) and smart cockpit setup.

The EREV will be Toyota’s fifth “electrified” vehicle, joining battery electric vehicles (BEVs), plug-in hybrids (PHEVs), hybrids (HEVs), and fuel-cell electric vehicles (FCEVs).

Unlike fully electric vehicles, EREVs have a small gas engine that acts as a generator to charge the battery when it gets low, extending driving range.

According to Nikkei, Toyota aims to produce 200,000 EREVs in China in 2027, and about 400,000 units in 2028.

We will have to wait until closer to launch for battery and powertrain specifics, but local reports suggest Toyota’s EREV will deliver a combined CTLC range of over 621 miles (1,000 km) on a full tank of gas and a full charge.

You can catch a glimpse of what appears to be the extended-range vehicle in the video GAC Toyota posted confirming the new EREV tech.

Since the Highlander 9X will be built in China, Toyota will not sell the EREV in the US. Instead, it will launch the fully electric Highlander BEV in the US in 2027.

The all-electric Toyota Highlander BEV will be available with front-wheel-drive and all-wheel-drive powertrains with two battery packs: 77 kWh or 95.8 kWh. The smaller (77 kWh) battery provides up to 287 miles of EPA-estimated range, while the larger (95.8 kWh) battery provides up to 320 miles in FWD models.

Like the outgoing version, the fifth-generation electric Toyota Highlander will offer three rows of seating and space for seven passengers.
